title: George Müller's orphans
hook: a preacher in Bristol cares for orphans and refuses to ask anyone but God for money

segments.voice: Yesterday: Florence Nightingale, who answered her call with night rounds and careful records. Your line was the lamp.

The children are sitting at long tables. The plates are out, the cups are out. There is no breakfast in the house, and no money to buy any. That's how a story told about George Müller begins. He stands, the story says, and gives thanks for the food anyway. Then a knock at the door: a baker who couldn't sleep, and who felt he should bake bread for the orphans. Then another knock: a milkman whose cart has broken down right outside, and who would rather give the milk away than let it spoil. Whether every detail happened just so, nobody can check now. But it's the kind of story his life produced.

George Müller was a German-born preacher who settled in Bristol, in England. By his own account, he had been a wild young man, a liar and a thief, before his faith took hold. In Bristol he saw children with no parents and nowhere to go, and he opened a home for them. Then more homes. Then large orphan houses on a hill outside the city. And he set himself a strange rule: he would ask no one for money. No appeals, no debts. He would bring every need to God in prayer and nobody else. He said he wanted the work to show that God hears prayer. He leaned on lines like this one in Philippians, in the King James Bible: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." Careful there means anxious. Don't be anxious; ask, and give thanks. And a psalm calls God "A father of the fatherless." Müller took that title at its word. But he didn't skip the paperwork. He kept careful records of the gifts that came in and the prayers he prayed, and he published accounts of the work. Some readers see those reports as a quiet way of letting donors know what was needed. His supporters say they were thanksgiving, a record of prayers answered. Both are honest readings. What's not in dispute is the rule itself: the children's needs were prayed for, not begged for.

Bring to mind something you need to ask someone for: help with a bill, a favor at work, an apology, a ride. Before asking, sit with the need itself, name it plainly, and notice what you're anxious about. If you pray, bring it to God first, with thanks, the way Philippians says; if you don't, hold it quietly and let the anxiety settle a little.
Müller. The Bristol preacher who opened homes for orphans and asked no one for money, bringing every need to God in prayer alone.
Your line: prayed for, not begged for. Thanks can come before the answer does. That's day nine hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Some Christian charities and missions still follow Müller's pattern of making needs known to God in prayer rather than appealing for funds, and his story is told in sermons and classes about prayer.
